Kiran Bazaar: Predicting Next-Month Food Price Spikes in Pakistan

CT-378 Machine Learning · Semester Project · Group: [names / roll numbers] · November 2026

Abstract

Food inflation is one of the most pressing household problems in Pakistan. We frame it as a binary classification task: will the retail price of a staple in a given city rise by more than 5 % next month? Using WFP / Pakistan Bureau of Statistics monthly prices for 13 staples in 5 cities (2014-2026, 9,568 city-item-months), combined with fuel, labour-wage and implied exchange-rate series, we engineered 26 leakage-free features and compared nine course algorithms under a chronological split with 5-fold time-series cross-validation. A Bagging ensemble of decision trees was selected on validation and reached ROC-AUC 0.82 and F1 0.49 on the held-out 2024-26 test period, against 0.62 / 0.33 for a persistence baseline. The model is deployed as a Streamlit app, a Hugging Face Space with model card, and a Flask REST API with an HTML front end.

1. Problem and motivation

Between 2022 and 2024 Pakistan's food prices rose faster than at any time in the dataset: atta in Lahore roughly tripled from its 2021 level at the 2023-24 peak. A household, NGO or ration-distribution programme that knew a month ahead that "atta in Lahore has a 78 % chance of jumping next month" could buy early or pre-position stock. Most prior ML work on this data predicts the price level (regression). We instead predict the event that matters to users: a spike above 5 % (≈ 15 % of city-item-months). This gives a clear target, meaningful metrics (F1, ROC-AUC) and an actionable output. A companion regression model supplies the expected next-month price.

2. Data collection

WFP Food Prices for Pakistan (HDX)14,345 monthly retail prices, 5 cities, 18 series, 2004-01 to 2026-09; sources FAO GIEWS/FPMA, PBSCC BY-IGOretrieved 2026-11-18
WFP Markets for Pakistan (HDX)market → province, district, latitude, longitudeCC BY-IGOretrieved 2026-11-18

We combine (i) the 13 food series (targets), (ii) the diesel, petrol and unskilled-wage series as cost-push drivers joined by city and month, (iii) a monthly USD/PKR rate implied by WFP's own conversion (Σprice / Σusdprice) and (iv) the market table. Data are market-level aggregates with no personal identifiers. The modelling window starts in 2014-01: before that only rice and wheat exist and the fuel/wage series are empty. Final table: 9,568 labelled rows × 26 features (4 categorical, 22 numeric) + 5 derived in-pipeline.

3. Exploratory data analysis

Fig. 1 - National price index of staples vs implied USD/PKR.
Fig. 2 - Spike rate by commodity and by year (class balance).

Seven EDA plots are in notebooks/01_eda.ipynb: coverage/missingness heatmap, distributions, trends, outliers, class balance, correlations, seasonality. Key findings: (1) prices are right-skewed and trend strongly with the rupee, so we use percentage changes rather than levels; (2) 40-50 % of months are missing for staples that start in 2013-15, and internal gaps are imputed inside the pipeline; (3) poultry and eggs spike 35-40 % of months while oil, ghee and milk rarely do; extreme changes are genuine market events and are kept; (4) the target is imbalanced (15 % positive) and its rate shifts over time (19 % in 2022-24); (5) the best single correlates are recent volatility and national momentum (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.27), so signals must be combined; (6) poultry and eggs are clearly seasonal.

4. Methodology

  • Features (past-only): 1/2/3/6/12-month changes, 6-month volatility, price vs 3/12-month mean and 12-month high, spikes in last 12 months, gap vs other cities, national momentum of the item, city food-basket momentum, diesel/petrol/wage changes, USD/PKR 1/3-month changes, city, province, category, month. Level features (log-price, PKR level) were tried and removed: they trend for 20 years and made linear models extrapolate (validation ROC-AUC of logistic regression rose from 0.51 to 0.71 after removal).
  • Pipeline (fitted on training data only): DerivedFeatures (cyclical month, relative momentum, fuel pressure, acceleration) → ColumnTransformer [median imputation + missing indicators + StandardScaler | most-frequent imputation + one-hot] → model.
  • Split: chronological 70/15/15 on whole months. Train 2014-01 to 2022-11 (6,646 rows), validation 2022-12 to 2024-09 (1,427), test 2024-10 to 2026-08 (1,495).
  • Models: baselines (class prior; persistence rule "jumped last month") + Logistic Regression, PCA+LR, KNN, Gaussian Naive Bayes, SVM (RBF), Decision Tree, Random Forest, Bagging, Gradient Boosting. Regression: Linear, Ridge, RF and Gradient Boosting regressors.
  • Tuning: GridSearchCV / RandomizedSearchCV with 5-fold TimeSeriesSplit, scored on ROC-AUC; class_weight="balanced" for imbalance. The best model on validation ROC-AUC is chosen. Its decision threshold is set on validation to maximise F1 (0.27, not 0.5), it is refit on train+validation, and it is evaluated once on test.
  • Unsupervised (notebook 03): PCA (10 components for 90 % variance), K-Means on per-series volatility profiles (k = 4) and Apriori association rules on monthly co-spike baskets.

Over/under-fitting. KNN (train ROC-AUC 1.00 vs val 0.69) and Gradient Boosting (0.96 vs 0.73) over-fit. Logistic Regression and Naive Bayes show small gaps but low training scores (high bias, under-fitting). Bagging (0.89 vs 0.76) balances the two and has the best validation ROC-AUC and PR-AUC. The 2022-24 inflation shock in validation (spike rate 19 % vs 15 %) explains why validation scores sit below CV scores.

Error analysis. The final model catches 59% of test spikes with 42% precision, versus 34 %/33 % for persistence. Its strongest signals are the national momentum of the item, its own last-month change and its recent spike history. Per commodity, test ROC-AUC is best for Poultry (0.77), Oil (cooking) (0.81), Lentils (moong) (0.88) and near chance for Rice (basmati, broken) (0.50), Eggs (0.52), Rice (coarse) (0.52). Part of the pooled 0.82 therefore comes from separating volatile from stable items. Fuel and FX features had slightly negative importance on 2024-26, when the rupee was stable. Masoor daal had no spikes in the test period. Regression: the Gradient Boosting regressor reaches test MAE 3.49 pp (R² 0.053) vs 3.60 pp for "no change". Monthly changes are close to a random walk, which supports the classification framing.

6. Deployment

Fig. 7 - Streamlit app: probability, verdict, expected price, history and "why" charts.
Fig. 8 - Hugging Face Space (Gradio).
Fig. 9 - Flask app (POST /predict + HTML front end).

All three apps share src/kiranbazaar/inference.py and load the same joblib pipelines. The user picks a city, a staple and an "as-of" month, and can optionally override this month's price change, diesel change and USD/PKR change for what-if analysis. Each app returns the spike probability, a verdict at the tuned threshold, the expected next-month price and a local explanation: the change in probability when each feature is reset to its median. The Flask API validates inputs (unknown city/commodity, bad month format, out-of-range or non-numeric overrides, non-JSON body) and returns HTTP 400 with a readable message. The front end also validates fields before sending.

7. Limitations and future work

  • Only five large cities and monthly granularity. Weekly PBS SPI data would allow earlier warnings and more cities.
  • No exogenous shock features (floods, wheat support-price announcements, import duties, bird-flu outbreaks, Ramadan/Eid shifting through the calendar).
  • Regime shifts change the base rate, so probabilities should be recalibrated periodically (e.g. retrain monthly, isotonic calibration).
  • Within-commodity skill is uneven. Per-commodity models or commodity-specific features (international palm-oil and wheat prices) are the next step.
